title: Economic Growth and the Rise of Forests
research_question: Does economic growth lead to increases in forest cover, and if so, through what mechanisms? Specifically, do rising incomes and population growth that increase demand for forest products cause forest expansion, or do alternative channels — such as agricultural productivity gains, rising wages, or demand for forests as environmental amenities — explain afforestation?
data_description: The authors assemble a village-level panel for rural India spanning 1971–1999, combining six sources: the 1970–71 NCAER ARIS household survey, the 1981–82 NCAER REDS, the 1991 Indian Census, the 1999 NCAER Village REDS, monthly weather data from the National Climate Data Center, and satellite spectral imagery (Landsat 1–3 MSS for 1971–1982, AVHRR NDVI for 1992, Landsat 7 ETM+ for 1999) covering roughly 250 geo-coded villages across sixteen major Indian states. Key variables include forest cover and biomass measured via the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index within a 10km radius, a Laspeyres index of high-yielding-variety crop yields (rice, wheat, corn, sorghum), agricultural wages, land prices, household income and fuel/paper/furniture expenditures, village population and household size, electrification, and road quality. The authors also use cross-country FAO forest-area data for 103 developing countries (1980, 1995) linked to ICP income and openness measures, plus Indian aggregate time series on wood consumption and fuelwood prices (1961–1999).
institutional_context: India provides a distinctive setting because it has been a largely closed economy since independence, with high tariffs on imported lumber and the relative non-tradability of fuelwood meaning that less than 1 percent of domestic wood consumption is imported. Fuelwood — the dominant forest product — has limited geographic mobility due to its low value-to-volume ratio, so local demand must be met by local forests, while labor and land are also largely village-bound. After decades of decline, India's officially designated forest land rose from 12.3 percent in 1951 to over 23 percent in 1999, coinciding with rising per-capita incomes, the spatially uneven Green Revolution (which advanced wheat yields earlier and rice yields later, varying by agro-climatic suitability), the Intensive Agricultural District Program, rural electrification and road expansion, and post-1970 forest management reforms including Joint Forest Management, which gave villagers stakes in timber proceeds.
